children.name: Project Description
children.reason:
Evaluation of the README file:

project_purpose:
Score (avg): 5.0
[QWEN] The README provides an excellent and thorough description of the project's purpose and usefulness. It opens with a clear statement: "CIB seven is a flexible framework for workflow and process automation" and further explains that "Its core is a native BPMN 2.0 process engine that runs inside the Java Virtual Machine." It goes on to describe the platform's capabilities (embedding in Java applications, Java EE 6 integration, Spring Framework compatibility) and provides a detailed component breakdown across four categories: Process Implementation and Execution, Process Design, Process Operations, and Human Task Management. The "A Framework" section explicitly addresses why it is useful by stating: "In contrast to other vendor BPM platforms, CIB seven strives to be highly integrable and embeddable. We seek to deliver a great experience to developers that want to use BPM technology in their projects." This is a comprehensive and compelling description of both what the project does and why it matters.

setup_instructions:
Score (avg): 2.0
[QWEN] The README does not contain any inline setup instructions. There are no prerequisites listed, no build steps, no installation commands, and no guidance on how to get the project running locally. The only references to setup are a "Getting Started" link in the top section (https://docs.cibseven.org/get-started/) and a "Tests" section that points to an external TESTING.md file. While linking to external getting-started documentation is a common and acceptable pattern, the README itself does not describe any setup instructions. A user reading only the README would not know how to build, configure, or run the project without navigating away to external resources.

info_project_status:
Score (avg): 1.0
[QWEN] The README contains no explicit statement about the project's status. There is no mention of whether the project is in active development, in maintenance mode, deprecated, or archived. While the presence of badges (manual latest, license, discussions), active links to an issue tracker, and a "Contributing" section implicitly suggest the project is ongoing, none of these constitute an explicit statement of project status. A reader cannot determine from the README alone whether the project is actively developed, in stable maintenance, or at risk of being abandoned.

info_maintainer:
Score (avg): 2.0
[QWEN] The README includes a "Contributing" section that references external contribution guidelines (CONTRIBUTING.md) for "how to raise issues and how to contribute code to our project," and the Community Extensions section mentions "our great open source community." Additionally, links to GitHub Discussions and the Issue Tracker are provided. However, the README does not explicitly name the organization or individuals responsible for maintaining the project. There is no "Maintainers" section, no list of core contributors, and no named maintainers. The use of "we" implies an organization but does not identify it. While the contribution pathway is referenced, the actual maintainership and contribution structure are not described in the README itself.

children.name: Project Structure
children.reason:
Project structure evaluation:

directory_organization:
Score (avg): 4.0
[QWEN] Question: "The project follows appropriate directory organization conventions for its technology stack (e.g., src/, tests/, docs/)." This is a large Java/Maven multi-module project with a JavaScript frontend, and it follows the expected conventions almost universally. Maven standards are respected throughout: each module has a pom.xml with src/main/java, src/main/resources, src/test/java and src/test/resources (e.g., engine/, commons/logging/, spin/dataformat-json-jackson/, model-api/bpmn-model/). Packaging-specific layouts are used correctly: src/main/webapp for WAR modules (distro/tomcat/webapp/, distro/wildfly/webapp/, webapps/assembly/src/main/webapp) and src/main/rar with META-INF/MANIFEST.MF for javaee/jobexecutor-rar. Root-level organization is conventional: mvnw/mvnw.cmd, parent/pom.xml, bom/, internal-dependencies/, LICENSE, NOTICE. Tooling is properly located: GitHub Actions under .github/workflows (14 workflow files) with ISSUE_TEMPLATE, Jenkins CI under .ci/ (config/, scripts/, per-pipeline Jenkinsfiles), and IDE/tooling settings under settings/ (eclipse, intellij-idea, maven). The frontend follows Node/npm conventions in webapps/frontend/ (package.json, package-lock.json, webpack.common.js/dev/prod, .eslintrc, .prettierrc, .babelrc, .npmrc, lib/ for SDK code, ui/ for apps, public/ for assets, scripts/). Points deducted for minor deviations: distro/run4/ duplicates the structure of distro/run/ with an unclear name; spring-boot-4-starter/ is a mostly empty scaffolding tree (subdirectories containing only pom.xml) that duplicates spring-boot-starter/; engine-rest/docs/ is named "docs" but actually contains a Node build pipeline (build.js, package.json, package-lock.json) for OpenAPI generation; and there is no top-level docs/ directory — documentation is scattered as READMEs per module (acceptable, but less conventional for a project of this scale).

naming_conventions:
Score (avg): 4.0
[QWEN] Question: "The project uses consistent naming conventions for files and directories (e.g., snake_case, camelCase)." The baseline naming is highly consistent. Module and directory names use kebab-case uniformly: model-api, engine-rest, dataformat-json-jackson, test-db-rolling-update, quarkus-extension, starter-webapp-core, tomcat10-runtime, integration-tests-engine. Workflow files (add-issue-to-project.yml, close-stale-issues.yml, java-dependency-check.yml), CI scripts (check-spring-alignment.sh, collect-alignment-facts.sh, alignment-lib.sh), and config files (matrices.yaml, stage-types.yaml, nexus-settings.xml) all follow the same kebab-case pattern. Conventional uppercase files appear where expected (README.md, CONTRIBUTING.md, SECURITY.md, TESTING.md, LICENSE, NOTICE, MANIFEST.MF, WEB-INF, META-INF). Java package directories use standard lowercase (org/cibseven/...), frontend JS files use camelCase per JS conventions (HttpClient.js, ResourceResolver.js, engineSelect.js), and index.js entry points are used consistently. Version-suffixed runtime directories follow a consistent pattern: tomcat-runtime/tomcat10-runtime (qa/), resources-tomcat/resources-tomcat10/resources-tomcat11 (qa/integration-tests-engine), and numbered fixtures test-fixture-11/20/21/22/30. Weaknesses: significant brand-name inconsistency — the project is "cib-seven", yet many artifacts retain the original "camunda" name (bom/camunda-bom, bom/camunda-only-bom, numerous camunda.cfg.xml and camunda.cfg.*.xml test configs, webapps/frontend/camunda-bpm-sdk-js/, org/camunda test packages under engine/ and qa/), while other artifacts use "cibseven" without a hyphen (distro/cibseven-welcome, start-cibseven.sh) and yet another uses "cib" (Jenkinsfile.cib). There is also a .yml vs .yaml extension mix (.github/workflows/*.yml and publiccode.yml vs .ci/config/matrices.yaml and default.yml/production.yml in distro/run/assembly/resources/), and a few outlier names (run4, spring-boot-4-starter) that break the established patterns.

separation_of_concerns:
Score (avg): 4.0
[QWEN] Question: "The project properly separates different concerns into appropriate directories (e.g., separating source, tests, configuration)." Separation of concerns is one of this project's strengths. Source and tests are separated in every module that has tests (src/main vs src/test, each with its own resources, e.g., logback-test.xml consistently placed under src/test/resources). Integration and acceptance tests are moved out of library modules into a dedicated top-level qa/ tree (integration-tests-engine with per-container source sets java-tomcat/java-wildfly/java-wildfly-servlet and matching resources-* directories, performance-tests-engine, large-data-tests, test-db-instance-migration, test-db-rolling-update) plus per-feature qa modules (clients/java/qa, distro/run/qa, quarkus-extension/engine/qa, spring-boot-starter/starter-qa). Shared test infrastructure is isolated in test-utils/ (archunit, assert, junit5-extension, junit5-extension-dmn, testcontainers). CI/CD configuration is separated from product code in .ci/ (Jenkins) and .github/workflows (GitHub Actions). Tooling and IDE configuration live in settings/ (eclipse/formatter.xml, intellij-idea/formatter.xml, maven/). Dependency management is cleanly split from code into parent/, bom/, internal-dependencies/, and per-ecosystem BOMs (commons/bom, connect/bom, spin/bom, engine-dmn/bom). Distribution and packaging are separated from library code in distro/ (per-target tomcat/wildfly/jboss modules, assembly.xml descriptors, license-book, sql-script, webjar) and engine-rest/assembly. Frontend concerns are separated into lib/ (SDK), ui/ (admin/cockpit/tasklist/welcome apps with their own tests/), public/ (static assets), and scripts/ (build helpers). Points deducted for a few overlaps: the parallel spring-boot-4-starter/ and spring-boot-starter/ trees duplicate a concern; distro/run4/ overlaps distro/run/; engine-rest/docs/ mixes a "docs" naming with build tooling; and the welcome webapp (distro/cibseven-welcome) contains checked-in binary assets (fonts, CSS, images) with no build or source-asset separation.

modularity:
Score (avg): 5.0
[QWEN] Question: "The project demonstrates good modularity with a logical breakdown of components or modules." The modular breakdown is exemplary. The core platform is decomposed into single-concern modules: model-api (xml-model, bpmn-model, cmmn-model, dmn-model), engine, engine-cdi, engine-spring (core, core-7), engine-dmn (engine, feel-api, feel-juel, feel-scala), engine-rest (engine-rest, engine-rest-openapi, engine-rest-openapi-generator, assembly), and engine-plugins (connect-plugin, identity-ldap, identity-scim, spin-plugin). Cross-cutting libraries are separate modules with clear scopes: commons (logging, testing, typed-values, utils, bom), spin (core, dataformat-all, dataformat-json-jackson, dataformat-xml-dom, bom), connect (core, http-client, soap-http-client, connectors-all, ai-agent, bom), plus juel, freemarker-template-engine, javaee (ejb-client, ejb-service, jobexecutor-ra, jobexecutor-rar), and database. Integration layers are isolated as their own module families: spring-boot-starter (starter, starter-client, starter-rest, starter-security, starter-test, starter-webapp, starter-webapp-core, starter-qa), quarkus-extension following the conventional Quarkus deployment/runtime/qa split, and clients/java (client, qa). Packaging is modularized per runtime target under distro/ (tomcat, wildfly with subsystem and modules, jboss, run, webjar, sql-script, license-book), keeping distribution artifacts decoupled from library code. QA and support tooling are separate modules (qa/*, test-utils/*, examples/invoice). A well-designed dependency-management hierarchy (parent/pom.xml, bom/, internal-dependencies/, and per-ecosystem BOMs such as connect/bom and spin/bom) supports consistent versioning across the dozens of modules. Nearly every module owns its own pom.xml and, where helpful, its own README.md and .gitignore, reflecting clear ownership. This is a textbook multi-module layout that makes independent build, test, and evolution of each component practical.

children.name: Security Policy
children.reason:
Evaluation of the SECURITY.md file:

security_contact_information:
Score (avg): 2.0
[QWEN] The document provides an actionable link for security reporting, but it does not provide clear, explicit contact information for security-related inquiries. It only says “See our Security Guide in the documentation” and “If you want to report a vulnerability please report it here through github,” linking to https://docs.cibseven.org/security/ and https://github.com/cibseven/cibseven/security/advisories/new. There is no direct security contact email, security team name, PGP key, alternate contact channel, or statement of how to reach the project for security questions that are not vulnerability reports. Therefore, the contact information is only partially helpful and not sufficiently clear.

vulnerability_reporting_process:
Score (avg): 3.0
[QWEN] The document clearly indicates where to report a vulnerability: “If you want to report a vulnerability please report it here through github,” with a direct link to https://github.com/cibseven/cibseven/security/advisories/new. This gives users an obvious first step. However, the process is not described in detail. The document does not explain what information should be included in a report, whether the report will be handled privately, what response or acknowledgment timeline to expect, how severity is assessed, or what happens after submission. It is acceptable but not fully detailed.

supported_versions:
Score (avg): 1.0
[QWEN] The document does not specify which versions of the software are currently supported with security updates. It contains no information about supported release versions, unsupported or end-of-life versions, update cadence, security patch policy, or version-specific support status. The only content is a reference to a security guide in the documentation and a GitHub link for reporting vulnerabilities, neither of which, as presented in the document, identifies supported versions.
